title: Sir Francis Drake (1540-1596)
body: Born in Devon, the son of a farmer and preacher, Drake began his naval career as a navigator on a small merchant ship before becoming the first Englishman to sail from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast of South America.
In 1577 he set off to circumnavigate the world aboard the Golden Hind, claiming land near present-day San Francisco for England along the way. He was knighted by Elizabeth I aboard the ship in 1581.
As Vice Admiral of the Navy, Drake helped defeat the Spanish Armada in 1588. He died of dysentery off Panama in 1596 and was buried at sea in a lead coffin that has never been found.

title: Admiral Lord Nelson (1758-1805)
body: Nelson joined the Navy as a midshipman aged just 12. He suffered from seasickness his whole career, lost the sight of his right eye at Calvi in 1794, and lost his right arm at Tenerife in 1797.

A brilliant tactician, Nelson destroyed Napoleon's fleet at the Battle of the Nile in 1798. At Copenhagen in 1801, ordered to break off action, he famously put his telescope to his blind eye and said he 'really did not see the signal'.
He was killed by a sniper's shot at his greatest victory, the Battle of Trafalgar, on 21 October 1805, aboard HMS Victory.

title: The Mary Rose (1509-1545)
body: Built at Portsmouth for Henry VIII, the Mary Rose was one of the first ships fitted with gun ports and was a favourite of the King, serving as flagship in two wars with France.
In 1545, while attempting to turn in battle, she flipped and sank with almost her entire crew of 700 lost, likely because she was overloaded and water poured in through her open gun ports.
The wreck was rediscovered in 1965 and raised in 1982, yielding 25,000 finds. She can be seen today in the Mary Rose Ship Hall in Portsmouth Dockyard, behind HMS Victory.

title: Battle of Trafalgar (1805)
body: On 21 October 1805, Nelson's fleet of 27 ships met a larger French and Spanish fleet of 33 ships off the coast of Spain. Nelson's radical battle plan split his fleet into two columns, attacking the enemy line head-on.
Before the battle, Nelson signalled the fleet: 'England expects that every man will do his duty.' The tactic worked decisively, but Nelson was shot and killed at the height of the action.
The victory guaranteed Britain's control of the oceans for over a century. Every year the Sea Cadets mark Trafalgar Day with a formal parade in Trafalgar Square.

title: Battle of Jutland (1916)
body: Fought over 31 May-1 June 1916 in the North Sea, Jutland was the only major naval battle of the First World War and the largest sea battle in history by ships engaged.

Britain's Grand Fleet, under Admiral Jellicoe, faced Germany's High Seas Fleet under Vice Admiral Scheer. Britain lost more ships and men - 14 ships and 5,672 sailors, against 11 German ships and 2,115 men.
Despite the heavier losses, the battle confirmed British naval supremacy: the German fleet never again seriously challenged the Royal Navy for control of the North Sea.

title: The Raid on Taranto (1940)
body: On the night of 11-12 November 1940, just 21 ageing Fleet Air Arm Swordfish biplanes attacked the Italian fleet at anchor in its main base at Taranto, Italy.
The raid crippled three Italian battleships for the loss of just two aircraft, instantly halving the strength of the Italian battlefleet.
The attack was studied closely by the Japanese navy, who drew on its lessons when planning their own carrier strike on Pearl Harbor just over a year later.

title: The Falklands Conflict (1982)
body: When Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982, Britain sent a task force of warships, submarines and requisitioned merchant ships some 8,000 miles to the South Atlantic.
The campaign saw the loss of HMS Sheffield, Ardent, Antelope, Coventry and Sir Galahad, but Sea Harriers destroyed 23 Argentine aircraft in air-to-air combat without a single loss of their own.
Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982, in what became one of the most remarkable feats of maritime power projection in modern history.
